Why stop there? Dave Schilling The move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk? Sun 30 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.22 EDT Share I magine driving in Italy, with its narrow, cobblestone streets and scooter enthusiasts. I find it hard enough to drive in Los Angeles , a city designed specifically with the automobile in mind. I’d probably squash a pedestrian or two trying to navigate Italian roads. The modern world is just too hectic for the ancient streets of Europe, so Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can: outlawing texting in crosswalks . The Italian government’s updated draft of its highway code proposes fines of €75 or more for anyone caught sending a DM, updating their LinkedIn, finishing Wordle on the fifth guess, or anything else phone-related that might make them miss an oncoming metal projectile. I’m sure most people will risk the slap on wrist to get that message off, but it at least sends a signal to the Italian people that paying attention to traffic is actually kind of important. Distracted pedestrians aren’t just a problem in Italy , though. If I’m turning right on a red light, chances are there will be someone inching slowly toward the intersection with their thumbs furiously smashing against the glass of their iPhone, oblivious to the fact that I am planning to drive into the parcel of land they are currently occupying. It’s not just that this behavior is dangerous. It’s also deeply annoying . I’m forced to pay attention for both of us, like I’m a guardian angel or the arbiter of whether you, the clueless phone person, live or die. Sure, I might briefly get off on the power trip of having such authority over our mutual safety, but I’d much rather be thinking about where to have dinner instead of how long I should wait to honk at the drooling simpleton preventing me from turning. Distracted Italian pedestrians who cross road while on phone could be fined under new code Read more I applaud the Italian government for their forward thinking. Actually, I think it’s time we criminalize more small annoyances. Such as … Using a ringtone Someone please explain to me why anyone bothers with leaving their ringer on. We are decades past the era when, for a dollar, you could buy that Crazy Frog song and impress your friends every time you got a call. Now, it’s just pure sonic detritus, clogging up our ears with aural poison – bleeps, bloops, pings and plops. When AMC Theaters tells an auditorium full of grown adults to silence their phones before a movie, all I can think is: “Unless they’re an on-call heart surgeon, their phone should always be silent.” Fine amount: $200 Interrupting me when I’m not done talking I understand and accept that I have a lot to say. I make my meager living from writing, so pontificating just comes naturally to me. Sometimes, I wish it didn’t. But most of the time, what I’m saying is pretty important and you should be listening. Not waiting for your turn. I just listened to you try to captivate me with a treatise on gender roles in Christopher Nolan’s films. I respected you, even if I didn’t want to. Either let me finish or you’re fined! Fine amount: $200 Not pushing in your chair when stepping away from a table at a restaurant Would you like to see the server at your favorite Olive Garden location break their tibia because you left your chair in the middle of a walkway? If that’s what you think of our restaurant industry workers, I’ve got a mind to go outside to my patio and bang on some pots and pans like it’s Covid lockdown to thank everyone carrying a plate of shrimp scampi who has to avoid rude customers. When you get up from your table, push in your chair. It takes two seconds and it could save a life … and a plate of delicious pasta. Fine amount: $250 Riding an electric scooter on the sidewalk I would like to remind everyone that scooters from companies such as Lime and Lyft explicitly say to not ride these vehicles on the sidewalk. The sidewalk is called a sidewalk because it, much like Nancy Sinatra’s boots , was made for walking. A motorized conveyance doesn’t belong on the sidewalk, especially ones that actually can get some real speed behind them. Use the bike lane, for God’s sake. Or take the bus. Or anything else, really. It’s just beyond dangerous to be tooling around on a scooter while people are trying to go about their business. I mean, what if I’m looking at my phone and texting? Shame on you, scooter guy. Tech CEO, Russian National Arrested in Idaho A Russian drone struck a Ukrainian train near the Polish border on Sunday, September 13, shortly after former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and senior European security officials had travelled along the same railway line. The strike hit the locomotive at Yahodyn, close to Ukraine’s border with Poland. No casualties were reported after passengers were evacuated, according to Ukrainian authorities. The incident came as Russia continued a broad aerial campaign against Ukraine involving drones and missiles. The timing has drawn particular attention because Johnson, senior European security officials and former CIA Director David Petraeus were among Western figures travelling through the area around the time of the attack. Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said the train carrying the European officials had departed earlier than expected because of continuing Russian strike threats. It said it was “quite possible” that the diplomatic train itself had been the intended target, although there is no independent confirmation that the Russian drone was specifically targeting Johnson or the other officials. Russia said it had targeted railway infrastructure. The drone struck approximately two kilometres from the Polish border, bringing the incident unusually close to NATO territory. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called an emergency meeting as officials assessed the incident. Reuters reported that the attack was part of a wider increase in Russian strikes around Ukrainian border crossings and logistical routes connected to European support for Ukraine. What happened to Boris Johnson’s train? Johnson and other European security officials were returning from the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv. The train they had used had passed through Yahodyn before the Russian strike. According to Ukrzaliznytsia, the schedule was changed and the train left the station earlier than originally planned because of the threat of Russian attacks. A separate train was subsequently struck. Passengers were ordered to evacuate roughly 15 minutes before the attack, according to Ukrainian railway officials. The drone hit the locomotive, but no passengers were reported killed or injured. Former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, who attended the Kyiv conference, said passengers on his train were ordered to prepare for evacuation before being told they could continue. The episode illustrates the security risks facing foreign officials travelling through Ukraine even on established diplomatic and civilian routes. But the location and timing have intensified concerns in Kyiv and European capitals about attacks on transport infrastructure used by civilians, diplomats and international delegations. The strike also occurred during one of the most intense periods of Russian aerial attacks in recent weeks. Reuters reported that Russia has increased its use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones as Ukraine faces shortages of air-defense interceptors. Russia struck Kyiv after U.S. peace envoys left The train attack follows another incident that has intensified scrutiny of Russia’s behavior around diplomatic activity. On Sept. 8, Russian missiles and drones struck Kyiv after a temporary halt in attacks that had coincided with the visit of U.S. peace negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The attack killed five people and injured dozens, according to Ukrainian authorities. Buildings including a school, clinic and residential structures were damaged. The U.S. envoys had left Kyiv two days earlier following meetings with Ukrainian officials as Washington sought to revive negotiations aimed at ending the war. The UN chief was in Kyiv when Russian missiles struck One of the clearest precedents came in April 2022, when United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres was visiting Kyiv. Guterres had travelled to Ukraine after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. On April 28, 2022, he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and visited Bucha, Borodianka and Irpin, where he condemned the destruction and called for accountability. While Guterres was in Kyiv, Russian rockets struck the city. The United Nations later recorded that Kyiv was hit by two rockets during the secretary-general’s visit. Guterres said he was shocked by the attack and said it demonstrated the need to end the war. Minsk agreements The Minsk agreements of 2014 and 2015 were designed to stop fighting in eastern Ukraine and establish a political framework for resolving the conflict. The agreements repeatedly failed to produce a durable ceasefire. Fighting continued in the Donbas, with Russia-backed separatists and Ukrainian forces accusing each other of violations. The broader breakdown became decisive in February 2022, when Putin recognized the Russian-backed separatist entities in Donetsk and Luhansk and then launched Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Budapest Memorandum The 1994 Budapest Memorandum is another major part of the dispute. Ukraine agreed to give up the nuclear weapons it inherited after the Soviet Union collapsed. In return, Russia, the United States and Britain committed to respect Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and existing borders and to refrain from the threat or use of force against Ukraine. Russia’s seizure of Crimea in 2014 and its subsequent military intervention in eastern Ukraine fundamentally breached those security assurances from Kyiv’s perspective. Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 went considerably further. The Black Sea grain agreement In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations helped broker the Black Sea Grain Initiative, allowing Ukrainian agricultural exports to move through designated maritime corridors despite the war. The agreement helped restore Ukrainian grain exports to global markets. Russia withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, arguing that commitments concerning Russian agricultural exports and fertilizer had not been adequately implemented. Ukraine and its Western partners disputed Moscow’s justification. Humanitarian corridors have also repeatedly failed Humanitarian arrangements have been another source of confrontation. During the early months of the full-scale invasion, attempts were made to establish corridors for civilians trapped in cities such as Mariupol. The safety of those corridors repeatedly became contested, with Ukraine accusing Russian forces of shelling evacuation routes and Russia making counter-accusations against Ukrainian forces. The United Nations has repeatedly stressed the need for safe humanitarian access rather than relying on informal assurances. EPA/Valda Kalnina https://theconversation.com/as-baltic-states-face-russian-hybrid-aggression-our-research-shows-what-europe-can-do-292757 https://theconversation.com/as-baltic-states-face-russian-hybrid-aggression-our-research-shows-what-europe-can-do-292757 Link copied Share article Share article Copy link Email Bluesky Facebook WhatsApp Messenger LinkedIn X (Twitter) Print article EU defence ministers assembled in Brussels on September 28 to try to formulate a response to increasing Russian aggression in Europe. The talks focused on Russia’s strategy of hybrid warfare – that is, hostile acts that fall below the threshold of actual war. These tend to include sabotage, disinformation, airspace violations, political interference and cyberwarfare. One part of Europe that has become familiar with these kinds of actions in recent years are the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Quite apart from being nervous because of their physical proximity to Russia, these countries have had to deal with regular acts of hybrid warfare for some years now. These tactics fall into what is often called the “grey zone” – they generally fall shy of the criteria needed to invoke Nato’s Article 5 clause of mutual self defence, which considers an attack on one member state as an attack on all. The increased use of hybrid actions has intensified in recent years, and the question of how to react to these grey zone threats has become a matter for debate inside Nato. The agreement is that a “game-changing” cyberattack could theoretically merit such a move . One of the difficulties is that these grey zone tactics come with a degree of plausible deniability. We saw this in 2014, when Russian troops entered parts of Ukraine, including Crimea, with no insignia (sometimes referred to as the “little green men”). Russia has also claimed that its aircraft and drones violating other countries’ airspaces have done so accidentally. And it’s often hard to determine who the malign player behind a serious cyberattack is and whether there are any links to a hostile government. The use of cyberattacks is a serious threat. Malicious cyberattacks can disable governance systems and telecommunications, and interfere with air traffic control and energy supplies. They can also be maliciously combined with real world conditions to amplified affect, for example, targeting heating systems in the winter. On occasions where attacks have been traced to Russia in the past, the Kremlin has blamed “online activists” and “non-state actors” . It is difficult to definitively confirm or disprove this in real time. ‘Little green men’: unidentified troops in Crimea in 2014. Russia initially it had deployed forces to the Ukranian penisula. EPA/Artus Shvarts Russia has been conducting cyberattacks against the Baltic nations for decades. But since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, these have formed part of a wider campaign of hybrid aggression – not only against the Baltic states but against a broader range of European states which have supported Ukraine. Geography suggests that the Baltic states would be the most vulnerable to a conventional military invasion in the event Russia wanted to challenge Nato’s resolve. But there is no particular evidence that Russia either intends to do so, nor is capable of doing so, given it remains bogged down in a heavily attritional conflict in Ukraine. But Russia’s hybrid actions have become bolder, including drone incursions, arson , and violent sabotage . There are signs that this is being increasingly recognised, such as in the speech to the United Nations general assembly by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham on September 22. Estonia’s ‘Bronze night’ My ongoing research project in collaboration with partners in the region has been exploring scenarios where hostile states can fuel hybrid crises and how democratic states can respond to them. One of the incidents we have examined in detail was what is known as the “Bronze night” in Estonia in 2007. This early example of hybrid conflict featured both cyberattacks and various other hostile acts, including the incitement of rioting, disinformation campaigns and economic pressure. The episode began after city authorities in Tallinn moved a Soviet-era statue, the Bronze Soldier, commemorating the soldiers of the Red Army. The statue was relocated from the centre of the city to a cemetery on the outskirts. While a symbol of pride to Estonia’s Russian-speaking minority, it symbolised Soviet occupation and oppression to many Estonians. The Soviet-era ‘Bronze Soldier’ statue was moved from the centre of Tallinn to the outskirts of the city. EPA/stringer The statue’s removal prompted outrage from many Russian speakers and a campaign of misinformation from Russia. News bulletins claimed the statue – and Russian war graves – had been destroyed. Two nights of rioting ensued. In Russia the Estonian embassy was besieged and the ambassador attacked. At the same time, Estonia was hit by a concerted campaign of cyberattacks, knocking out banks, media outlets and government departments through a series of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. These events prompted Estonia’s government to set up a cyber defence unit. Estonia also now hosts Nato’s cooperative cyber defence centre of excellence. Baltic defence Nearly two decades on, what is remarkable is how consistent these hybrid attacks have remained. But as technology continues to develop and expand, so do the grey zone opportunities – whether they are cyberattacks or social media powered disinformation campaigns. Our ongoing research is developing war-gaming scenarios to support decision-makers in responding to these hybrid threats and the crisis events they can trigger. Through our work, we highlight the multiple ways that Moscow has, and continues to exploit the grey zone, drawing upon Baltic experience, while also highlighting similar hostile Russian tactics elsewhere in our scenarios. The project explores how policymakers, local and national governments, and organisations can better prepare for such campaigns. The aim is to develop an open-access tool which will be supported by detailed guidance and case studies which will help in training policy development and operational planning. The Baltic way of dealing with these crises is broadly speaking defined through recognition of the problem, unflinching attribution to Moscow, outspoken support for Ukraine, and a refusal to be intimidated by the Kremlin. This was perhaps best summed up by the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, in May. Responding to what he called “absolutely clear lies,” from Moscow that his country was allowing Ukraine to launch drone attacks against Russia, with the implicit threat that Russia could attack Latvia in response, Rinkēvičs told the state broadcaster that: “We are in a new reality. Such attempts in these anxious times – both internationally and domestically – will and must be treated with a cool head.” Russia Estonia Latvia Lithuania Baltic states Cyberattacks Hybrid warfare cyberwarfare Ukraine invasion 2022 Alex Hardy , University of Liverpool Author Alex Hardy Postdoctoral Research Associate, Communication and Media, University of Liverpool Disclosure statement Alex Hardy receives funding from NetworkPlus for Analytical Behavioural Science (NABS+) in Security and Defence.
